# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Most quantitative work on how generative AI bears on the labour market starts from a measure of what a language model *could* do. Occupations and their tasks are scored for theoretical exposure, by human raters or by a model, and those scores are aggregated to occupations, industries and regions [@eloundou2024gpts; @felten2021occupational; @webb2020impact]. Such scores describe capability, not use. They are silent on whether anyone actually brings a given task to a model and, if so, on how the work is shared between person and machine. The Anthropic Economic Index (AEI) offers a different kind of record [@handa2025economic; @anthropic2026economicindex]. Its data are conversations matched to O\*NET tasks, published in successive releases from {{< var design.release.r1 >}} to {{< var design.release.r6 >}} (@tbl-releases; @sec-app-supplementary). Each release reports not only which tasks appear in observed usage but also the *collaboration pattern* of those conversations: whether the user hands the task over or works through it with the model. That second dimension is a behavioural variable, and it is the one this paper studies. It is also a record of usage on a single provider's platforms, not of the population of people at work, and every statement below is about that usage; the scope and the drift of the platform across releases are discussed in @sec-limitations.

The AEI classifies conversations into five collaboration patterns and groups them into two buckets. *Automation* covers the directive and feedback-loop patterns, in which the user asks for a finished product or relays results back for the model to act on; *augmentation* covers task iteration, learning and validation, in which the user refines, studies or checks the work [@handa2025economic]. We call the automation share *delegation* and the augmentation share *collaboration*, and we read the distinction through the psychology of trust in automation. @parasuraman1997humans describe how people use, misuse and disuse automated systems, and @lee2004trust argue that appropriate reliance requires trust calibrated to a system's actual capability. Work on algorithm aversion and appreciation finds that the willingness to defer to an algorithm varies with the stakes, with whether the algorithm has been seen to err, and with the kind of judgement involved [@dietvorst2015algorithm; @logg2019algorithm]. These literatures suggest where delegation should be lower (tasks and occupations where errors are costly or human judgement is prized), where checking should be more common, and how reliance might change as users gain experience. The RQ1 hypotheses are written as tests of those suggestions on observed usage rather than on survey responses or laboratory choices (@sec-literature).

The paper makes three contributions. First, it documents the behavioural structure of delegation: in which occupations and for which tasks work is handed to the model, how that differs across countries, and whether the measured pattern changes across releases (@sec-rq1). Second, it turns task-level usage and collaboration shares into industry-level exposure measures that keep *usage* apart from *delegation* and *augmentation*, built for the {{< var design.n_industries >}} Fama–French industries through occupation and industry crosswalks (@sec-data), and benchmarks them against theoretical exposure scores to ask how far "could" and "does" are apart (@sec-rq2). Third, it tests whether the repricing of industries in equity markets since the launch of ChatGPT on {{< var design.seal_date >}} lines up with observed delegation rather than theoretical exposure (@sec-markets). Along the way the paper builds the measurement apparatus that the AEI's changing release formats require: a harmonised panel of releases, a record of the measurement regime behind each one (@tbl-regimes; @sec-app-supplementary), and a replication package that rebuilds every number from the raw downloads (@sec-app-replication).

The analysis was pre-registered. The protocol, tagged {{< var pap.tag >}} in the repository and dated {{< var pap.date >}}, fixes every confirmatory specification, decision rule and robustness row before the confirmatory outcomes were read; it is reproduced in @sec-app-pap and summarised in @sec-methods. There are two confirmatory families. For RQ1 the family-wise level of {{< var design.alpha.rq1_total >}} is split: H2 is tested on its own at {{< var design.alpha.rq1_h2 >}}, and H1, H3 and H4 form a Holm family at {{< var design.alpha.rq1_family >}} [@holm1979simple]. For RQ3, H5 and H5b form a Holm family whose step levels are {{< var design.alpha.h5_first >}} and {{< var design.alpha.h5_second >}}. H5 and H5b are tested against the frozen historical pattern of cross-industry slopes for the same exposure vector, estimated on windows that end before the market seal date, rather than against zero; the test against zero is kept as a labelled secondary result. The historical slopes are not centred at zero, and a test against zero over-rejects across the historical windows, so a rejection here means a departure from that pattern, a narrower claim than the approved wording of H5 (@sec-methods); the recentring was proposed after those pre-seal rejection rates had been seen, as @sec-app-disclosures records. RQ2 is descriptive and carries no test, and H6 is exploratory. Every departure from the protocol after the tag is listed in @sec-app-deviations, and the disclosures are in @sec-app-disclosures.

The protocol also contains a rule about what the market evidence can bear. The pre-registered power analysis gives a minimum detectable effect (MDE) for the primary H5 test of {{< var d11.primary_mde >}} pp of annualised alpha per standard deviation of exposure, at the first Holm step and on the frozen historical null scale. Decision D11 states that if this MDE exceeds {{< var design.plausibility_pp >}} pp per standard deviation, RQ3 is reported as "what the market evidence can and cannot yet say", and the paper is led by RQ1 and RQ2. The MDE exceeds the threshold, so the rule fires. The threshold was written into the project plan before the power analysis was first run, but it became binding only when the protocol was signed, by which time the MDE was known; a reader should treat it as a threshold confirmed with the MDE in view (@sec-methods). The market tests are still run and reported in full, with the MDE beside each result (@sec-markets).

For RQ1 (@sec-rq1, @tbl-rq1-confirmatory-table), H1 is {{< var rq1.h1.decision_text >}}: the null that either coefficient is zero is not rejected at {{< var rq1.holm.h1 >}} (intersection–union p = {{< var rq1.h1.p >}}). Within task families, the automation share changes by {{< var rq1.h1.beta_e >}} pp per year of required education (CI [{{< var rq1.h1.human_education_years_mean.ci_low >}}, {{< var rq1.h1.human_education_years_mean.ci_high >}}], p = {{< var rq1.h1.human_education_years_mean.p >}}) and by {{< var rq1.h1.beta_w >}} pp per unit of log wage (CI [{{< var rq1.h1.log_wage.ci_low >}}, {{< var rq1.h1.log_wage.ci_high >}}], nominal p = {{< var rq1.h1.log_wage.p >}}). The wage coefficient is opposite in sign to H1's prediction and is not significant at its Holm level, so it neither supports nor contradicts H1; one pre-registered robustness row, R24 r5, takes the H1 p-value below its Holm level with both coefficients negative, and it changes no decision. H2 is {{< var rq1.h2.decision_text >}}: the release-level co-condition fails. The within-task trend in the automation share over r2–r5 is {{< var rq1.h2.beta >}} pp per year (task-clustered CI [{{< var rq1.h2.trend.ci_low >}}, {{< var rq1.h2.trend.ci_high >}}], p {{< var rq1.h2.p_cluster >}}), but the release-level wild bootstrap gives p = {{< var rq1.h2.p_wild >}} against a level of {{< var rq1.holm.h2 >}}. The measured rise is a single r2-to-r3 step followed by a fall (@fig-rq1-h2-release-effects); leaving out r2 reverses the sign of the trend, to {{< var diag.h2.leave_out_release_r2.beta >}} pp per year (a post-result diagnostic, PAP §11 D-3; exploratory; not a decision); and the r2-to-r3 step coincides with a change in the base of classified conversations, so classifier or platform drift cannot be separated from behaviour. Rows R22 (`api_r3_r5`) and R23 run the other way, and the balanced-panel rule removes {{< var diag.h2.balancing_removed.n_tasks >}} tasks holding {{< var diag.h2.balancing_removed.usage_share_pct >}} % of usage (descriptive). H3 is {{< var rq1.h3.decision_text >}}: the null that γ is zero is not rejected at {{< var rq1.holm.h3 >}}, with γ = {{< var rq1.h3.gamma >}} pp of validation share in high-error-cost occupations (CI [{{< var rq1.h3.error_cost.ci_low >}}, {{< var rq1.h3.error_cost.ci_high >}}], p = {{< var rq1.h3.error_cost.p >}}). H4 is {{< var rq1.h4.decision_text >}}: the joint Wald test of the two country-level coefficients gives p {{< var rq1.h4.p_wald >}} at {{< var rq1.holm.h4 >}}. Conditional on task mix, the automation share changes by {{< var rq1.h4.b1 >}} pp per unit of log AUI (CI [{{< var rq1.h4.log_aui.ci_low >}}, {{< var rq1.h4.log_aui.ci_high >}}]) and by {{< var rq1.h4.b2 >}} pp per unit of log GDP per working-age person (CI [{{< var rq1.h4.log_income.ci_low >}}, {{< var rq1.h4.log_income.ci_high >}}]). The two regressors are strongly correlated across countries, since both share the working-age population denominator, so b₁ and b₂ are only weakly separable one by one, although their joint test is not.

RQ2 is descriptive (@sec-rq2). Across the Design B industries, the Spearman correlation between delegation exposure and the human-rated exposure of @eloundou2024gpts is {{< var rq2.b.z_delegation.z_eloundou.rho >}} (industry-bootstrap CI [{{< var rq2.b.z_delegation.z_eloundou.ci.lo >}}, {{< var rq2.b.z_delegation.z_eloundou.ci.hi >}}]; @tbl-rq2-could-vs-does-b, @fig-rq2-could-vs-does). Industries rated most exposed also tend to show the most delegation, and the industries whose ranks differ most between the two measures are listed in @tbl-rq2-rank-gaps-eloundou (@sec-app-supplementary). Two qualifications sit beside this number. The correlation inherits the same OEWS occupation-to-industry weights on both sides, so part of it is common occupational mix; and it depends on the D3 assumption, under which occupations unpublished in the AEI are assigned zero usage by assumption rather than measured as zero, with R3 lowering it most, to {{< var rob.r03.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.estimate >}}. As to timing, Design B's OEWS {{< var vintage.oews.primary >}} weights were released on {{< var design.s1.oews_release >}}, after the {{< var design.formation >}} formation date and inside the return window, and the O\*NET {{< var vintage.onet.primary >}} links postdate formation; Design B is out of sample in AEI data only and is not strictly real-time. The strict real-time row, R32, uses OEWS {{< var vintage.oews.r32 >}} weights and is run for the market tests only (@sec-robustness).

Under D11, RQ3 is reported as what the market evidence can and cannot yet say (@sec-markets, @tbl-rq3-confirmatory). H5 is {{< var rq3.h5.decision_text >}}, and H5b is {{< var rq3.h5b.decision_text >}}. Over the return window from {{< var design.window.start >}} to {{< var design.window.end >}}, the cross-industry slope of annualised alpha on delegation exposure is {{< var rq3.h5.b_pp2 >}} pp per standard deviation (p = {{< var rq3.h5.p >}} against the frozen historical pattern), and {{< var rq3.h5b.b_pp2 >}} pp per standard deviation once theoretical exposure is controlled for (p = {{< var rq3.h5b.p >}}). In the pre-registered wording: {{< var rq3.h5.wording >}} {{< var rq3.h5b.wording >}} The robustness rows that move the H5 slope most are R7 (dropping Hardw, Softw and Chips), R12 (ranks) and R5 (equal-weighted returns), and for H5b they are R12, R7 and R6 (FF30); all are reported as robustness and none changes a decision (@sec-robustness). The timing caveat stated for RQ2 applies here too: Design B is out of sample in AEI data only and is not strictly real-time. Under R32, the strict real-time row, the slopes are {{< var rob.r32.h5.estimate >}} and {{< var rob.r32.h5b.estimate >}} pp per standard deviation, and R1 is reported throughout as look-ahead. A test with this MDE can detect only a large departure from the historical pattern, and the non-rejections are statements about what this window can and cannot resolve. Exploratory: H6 compares how much industries discuss AI in their 10-K filings with how much they are observed to use it, and sits outside every testing family (@sec-markets).

The paper proceeds as follows. @sec-literature reviews the literatures on exposure measurement, on generative AI at work, on trust in automation and on the pricing of technology exposure. @sec-data describes the AEI releases, the crosswalks and the construction of the industry exposure indices. @sec-methods sets out the pre-registration, the testing families and the inference for each hypothesis. @sec-rq1 reports the behavioural results, @sec-rq2 the comparison of observed and theoretical exposure, and @sec-markets the market evidence together with the exploratory analyses. @sec-robustness summarises the pre-registered robustness rows, whose full tables are in @sec-app-robustness-tables. @sec-limitations discusses what the design cannot establish, and @sec-conclusion concludes.
